newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Spread of HIV in Asia may fuel TB epidemic - WHO.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Spread of HIV in Asia may fuel TB epidemic - WHO.

text.p: The rapid spread of HIV in the Asia Pacific threatens to exacerbate an existing epidemic of tuberculosis (TB) in the region, the World Health Organisation (WHO) warned on Monday.
Asia is already home to about two thirds of the world's active cases of TB, an airborne lung disease that claims about three million lives each year.
While sub-Saharan Africa has so far suffered most from the combined effects of HIV and TB, the dual epidemic promises an even more vicious attack in Asia, according to WHO.
"TB is a growing threat, particularly because of the HIV epidemic and also because it never went away," said Thomas Frieden, a WHO regional spokesman based in New Delhi.
"The spread of HIV in the region makes it particularly urgent that we implement TB controls rapidly and effectively," Frieden told Reuters.
TB was almost eradicated in western countries after the development of effective treatments and vaccines in the 1950s, although it has started to creep back with rising levels of HIV.
In Asia, however, the disease was never tackled and in countries such as India up to half the population carries the TB infection.
Frieden, who is attending a WHO regional conference in Sydney, said HIV destroys a person's immune system, increasing the chance of them developing TB.
As more and more people become HIV infected, the TB disease is spread more rapidly to others, widening the epidemic.

Michael Levy, of the WHO's global tuberculosis programme, said about one in 10 infected people would normally develop active TB. However, the presence of HIV increased the rate of developing active TB about twenty-fold.
Health authorities are also fighting the dangers of drug resistant tuberculosis due to careless treatment.
Drugs to counter TB are well known and cheap, costing as little as US$11 in some countries, but patients must finish a lengthy programme of antibiotics.
Levy said in countries with poor controls on drugs, such as the Philippines and India, people bought drugs for as long as their money lasted or until they felt better.
"If someone doesn't take the full course of treatment they may die or they may develop a drug resistant strain of TB which they can spread to others," warned Frieden.
Already, however, 50 million people worldwide are believed to have developed drug resistant TB out of the 1.7 billion people estimated to be infected worldwide, Frieden said.
